---
title: "Handwritten digits as mixtures of archetypes"
description: "What if every handwritten digit were a recipe made of a few pure ones? A hands-on example of archetypal analysis with 1,797 digit images and the Python library archetypes."
date: "2026-10-07"
categories: [archetypal analysis, python]
draft: true
---

In [the previous note](/notes/archetypal-analysis/) we described a cloud of dots as mixtures of a few extreme cases. Dots on a page are easy to picture, but archetypal analysis works on anything that can be turned into numbers. A picture is exactly that, and the results are surprisingly easy to read.



## A picture is a table of numbers

A grey image is a table of numbers: one per pixel, from 0 (white) to 16 (black) here. The digits in this note are tiny, 8×8 pixels, so each one is 64 numbers.

::: {#dcc5dfac .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27}
![A handwritten 3 and the table of numbers behind it: one number per pixel, from 0 (white) to 16 (black).](index_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.svg){fig-alt='An animation of a tiny 8 by 8 pixel picture of the digit 3 with the grey level of every pixel written on it, while a green square visits the pixels one by one.'}
:::
:::


Think of every digit as a dot in a space with 64 directions instead of two. We cannot draw that space, but the ideas of the previous note work in it exactly the same way. We will use 1,797 handwritten digits, a small public collection that comes with scikit-learn.

::: {#a0b5fa0c .cell execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Sixty of the 1,797 handwritten digits. The algorithm will never be told which digit is which.](index_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.svg){fig-alt='A grid of sixty tiny pictures of handwritten digits.'}
:::
:::


## Ten pure digits

Let us ask archetypal analysis for 10 archetypes. It only sees the pictures, never which digit each one is. Watch how they emerge: the algorithm starts from ten random digits and, iteration after iteration, moves them towards the extremes. For a while they get blurry, because an archetype is a mixture of real digits and early on it mixes many of them. Then they sharpen again into ten different digits.

::: {#a13f7566 .cell execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29}
![Archetypes emerging. The algorithm starts from 10 random digits; as it moves them towards the extremes they blur for a while and then sharpen into 10 different digits. On the left, the average of all the digits, for comparison. At the end, under each archetype, the digit it looks like most.](index_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.svg){fig-alt='An animation of ten small pictures of digits that first become blurry and then sharpen again into clear, different digits, next to a grey smudge, the average digit.'}
:::
:::


They look like digits. The *average* digit, on the left, is a grey smudge, because it mixes everything. The archetypes are crisp for the reason we saw in the previous note: each one is built from real digits, about 11 of them, so it keeps their sharp strokes.

Nobody told the algorithm that there are digits from 0 to 9, and yet its archetypes look like the digits 0\, 1\, 2\, 3\, 4\, 5\, 6\, 7\, 9. Two of them look like the digit 1, and none looks like the digit 8.

## A digit without an archetype

If no archetype looks like an 8, can archetypal analysis still describe an 8? Of course: an 8 is a mixture. This is the recipe of one of them.

::: {#64192342 .cell execution_count=6}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30}
![Building an 8 from archetypes. Each ingredient adds its percentage to the mixture, until the mixture looks like the real 8.](index_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.svg){fig-alt='An animation in which three pictures of archetypes appear one after another, each with its percentage, while a picture on the right gradually turns into the handwritten 8 on the left.'}
:::
:::


This 8 is mostly a mixture of the archetypes that look like the digits 3\, 6\, 9, whose round strokes together make up an 8. It is a recipe like the ones in the previous note: percentages that add up to 100%.

## Sliding between archetypes

Because every digit is a mixture, we can also run the recipe in reverse and create digits by choosing the percentages ourselves. In the animation, the dot of the previous note has become a picture. At an archetype we see that pure digit; in between, the shapes melt into one another.

::: {#0a4ee140 .cell execution_count=7}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31}
![Mixing three archetypes. The picture on the left is the mixture given by the percentages on the right.](index_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.svg){fig-alt='An animation of a picture that gradually changes from one digit to another while three bars show how much of each of three archetypes it contains.'}
:::
:::


## What is each digit made of?

We can also ask, for every real digit, which archetypes it is made of. Each row shows the average recipe of one digit, from 0 to 9, and each column is one archetype.

::: {#4b242c17 .cell execution_count=8}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32}
![The average recipe of every real digit (rows) in terms of the 10 archetypes (columns), in percent. Dark green means that the archetype is a large part of that digit.](index_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.svg){fig-alt='An animation of a table with ten rows, one per digit, and ten columns, one per archetype, whose cells appear row by row, shaded from white to green according to their percentage.'}
:::
:::


Most digits are mainly their own archetype. The most mixed one is the 8, the digit that has no archetype of its own: no single archetype is more than 26% of it. That is what a mixture looks like in practice.

## How good is the description?

With 10 archetypes, 43% of the variation of the digits is left unexplained, and it only goes down slowly as we add more.

::: {#977efa03 .cell execution_count=9}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=33}
![Unexplained variation against the number of archetypes. Unlike the cloud of athletes in the previous note, there is no clear elbow: pictures are much richer than a cloud of dots.](index_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.svg){fig-alt='An animation of a line chart that is drawn point by point: it starts high and decreases slowly as the number of archetypes grows from 2 to 30.'}
:::
:::


Pictures are much richer than a cloud of dots, so it takes many archetypes to rebuild them faithfully. That is not what archetypal analysis is for. If all you want is to rebuild images with as few numbers as possible, other methods, such as PCA, do it better. Archetypes trade some accuracy for something else: a small set of pure, readable cases. Here, ten of them are enough to see, at a glance, the different ways of writing the digits.

## Try it yourself

The `archetypes` library follows the scikit-learn conventions, so using it feels familiar. Install it with `pip install archetypes`.

::: {#d3c336f0 .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from archetypes import AA
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits

X = load_digits().data / 16                     # 1,797 digits of 64 pixels, from 0 to 1
aa = AA(n_archetypes=10, random_state=3)
weights = aa.fit_transform(X)                   # one recipe per digit: 10 percentages that add up to 1
archetypes = aa.archetypes_                     # the 10 pure digits, 64 pixels each
```
:::


`weights` has one row per digit and `archetypes` has one row per archetype. A different `random_state` starts the algorithm elsewhere and can give slightly different archetypes. To see an archetype as a picture, reshape its 64 numbers into an 8×8 table: `archetypes[0].reshape(8, 8)`.

## In short

- A picture is a table of numbers, so archetypal analysis can describe it as a **mixture of archetypes** too.
- The archetypes of the digits are **real-looking digits**, because each one is built from real pictures.
- A digit that has no archetype, like the 8, is simply **a mixture of several**.
- It is not the best tool to rebuild pictures, but it is a very good one to **read** them.
